tracks.name: Pipelines
tracks.description: Every push gets the same answer, in minutes.

lessons.title: 1. Your first pipeline
lessons.summary: Install from the lockfile, then check what you would block a merge on.

activities.title: A workflow that gates the merge
activities.instruction: A CI workflow runs on pull requests and pushes. It installs dependencies reproducibly with `npm ci`, then runs the checks you actually trust: lint, typecheck, tests. If any step exits non-zero, the job fails and the branch is not mergeable.
activities.example:
name: ci

on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm test

activities.title: ci or install
activities.question: Why does CI use `npm ci` rather than `npm install`?
choices: It installs exactly what the lockfile pins and fails if they disagree
It installs faster because it downloads fewer packages
It updates dependencies to their newest patch versions
activities.answer: It installs exactly what the lockfile pins and fails if they disagree
activities.explanation: Reproducibility is the point. If `package.json` and the lockfile drift, `npm ci` fails instead of quietly producing a different tree than the one tested on your machine.

activities.title: Add the test step
activities.instruction: In the `test` job, check out the repo, install with `npm ci` and run `npm test`.

teaching.text: CI is a shared, automatic judge. Its value comes from being the same judge for every pull request, so 'it works on my machine' stops being an argument.

- run: npm ci
- run: npm test
Make the required checks fast. A ten-minute pipeline gets bypassed; a two-minute one gets respected.

lessons.task: Write a job that installs and tests on every pull request.
lessons.starterCode:
name: ci

on:
  pull_request:

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      # checkout, install, test
hints: Use `actions/checkout` first, then `npm ci`, then `npm test`.

- uses: actions/checkout@v4
- run: npm ci
- run: npm test
lessons.solution:
name: ci

on:
  pull_request:

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm test
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Which check would you refuse to let a teammate bypass on a Friday deploy?

lessons.title: 2. Fast feedback
lessons.summary: Cache what rarely changes and test the versions you support.

activities.title: Cache dependencies, matrix the runtime
activities.instruction: Most of a cold pipeline is dependency download. Cache the package manager's directory keyed by the lockfile hash, and use a matrix to run the same steps on the runtime versions you claim to support. Fail-fast keeps a red build from burning time on the rest.
activities.example:
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        node: [20, 22]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node }}
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test

activities.title: Cache invalidation
activities.question: What should the dependency cache key include so stale packages are never restored?
choices: A hash of the lockfile
The current date
The branch name only
activities.explanation: The cache must change exactly when dependencies change. A date busts it constantly; a branch name restores one branch's cache into another.

activities.title: Add a matrix and caching
activities.instruction: Run the job on Node 20 and 22 using a matrix, with npm caching enabled.

teaching.text: Pipeline time is developer time multiplied by change frequency. Cache dependencies, shard slow test suites, and stop on the first failure unless you need the full matrix.

strategy:
  matrix:
    node: [20, 22]
with:
  node-version: ${{ matrix.node }}
  cache: npm
Test the versions you actually run in production. A matrix over five versions nobody deploys is a slower pipeline for false confidence.

lessons.task: Add a Node version matrix and dependency caching to the job.
lessons.starterCode:
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test
hints: `strategy.matrix` defines the values; reference them with `${{ matrix.node }}`.

strategy:
  matrix:
    node: [20, 22]
# then node-version: ${{ matrix.node }} and cache: npm
lessons.solution:
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        node: [20, 22]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node }}
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why can a cache that never invalidates be worse than no cache at all?

lessons.title: 3. Build once, promote
lessons.summary: The thing you tested is the thing you deploy, byte for byte.

activities.title: Tag by commit, deploy by digest
activities.instruction: Build the container image once in CI and tag it with the commit SHA. Promote that same image through staging and production by digest. Rebuilding per environment produces a different artifact, and then you are testing one thing and shipping another.
activities.example:
docker build -t ghcr.io/acme/api:$GITHUB_SHA .
docker push ghcr.io/acme/api:$GITHUB_SHA

# Deploy the exact digest that passed staging
docker pull ghcr.io/acme/api@sha256:9f2c1a...

activities.title: Rebuilding for production
activities.question: Your pipeline builds a fresh image for each environment. What is the risk?
choices: The production image may differ from the one that passed tests
The image will be larger
Nothing — the Dockerfile is the same
activities.answer: The production image may differ from the one that passed tests
activities.explanation: Base image tags move, build args differ, and caches drift. A commit SHA tag plus promotion of the tested digest removes the gap.

activities.title: Tag and push the image
activities.instruction: Build the image tagged with `$GITHUB_SHA` and push it to the registry.

teaching.text: An artifact is anything you deploy: a container image, a bundle, a migration bundle. Its name should identify its source exactly; a mutable tag like `latest` cannot.

docker build -t ghcr.io/acme/api:$GITHUB_SHA .
docker push ghcr.io/acme/api:$GITHUB_SHA
Never deploy `latest` to production. Rollback needs a previous, named artifact to return to.

lessons.task: Build and push an image tagged with the commit SHA.
lessons.starterCode: # Build the image and push it
hints: Use the commit SHA as the tag in both commands.

docker build -t ghcr.io/acme/api:$GITHUB_SHA .
docker push ghcr.io/acme/api:$GITHUB_SHA
lessons.solution:
docker build -t ghcr.io/acme/api:$GITHUB_SHA .
docker push ghcr.io/acme/api:$GITHUB_SHA
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why is a SHA tag more useful than `latest` when you need to roll back?

tracks.name: Deployments
tracks.description: Ship without dropping requests or corrupting data.

lessons.title: 4. Config and environments
lessons.summary: Same artifact, different settings — never different code.

activities.title: Config from the platform
activities.instruction: Configuration belongs in the environment: database URLs, feature endpoints, log levels. Secrets go in the platform's secret store, never in the repository or the image. Validate the required values at boot so a bad deploy fails immediately instead of on the first request.

activities.title: Where secrets live
activities.question: Where should a production database password live?
choices: In the platform's secret store, injected as an environment variable
In a committed `.env.production` file
Baked into the image at build time
activities.answer: In the platform's secret store, injected as an environment variable
activities.explanation: A committed file is in history; a value baked into the image is in the registry and every cache layer. Both spread the secret far beyond the environment that needs it.

activities.title: Fail fast at boot
activities.instruction: Check `DATABASE_URL`, `SESSION_SECRET` and `REDIS_URL` at startup and throw listing any that are missing.

teaching.text: The same image should run in staging and production. If the code differs, the staging test tells you less than you think.

const missing = required.filter((name) => !process.env[name]);
if (missing.length) throw new Error(`Missing env: ${missing.join(', ')}`);
Log the names of missing variables, never their values. An error message is a log line too.

lessons.task: Validate required environment variables at startup.
lessons.starterCode:
// Validate the environment before the server starts
const required = ['DATABASE_URL', 'SESSION_SECRET', 'REDIS_URL'];
hints: Filter the required names by whether they are set.

const missing = required.filter((name) => !process.env[name]);
if (missing.length) throw new Error(`Missing env: ${missing.join(', ')}`);
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why should a missing environment variable crash the process at boot?

lessons.title: 5. Migrations in the deploy
lessons.summary: Old and new code run at the same time, so schema changes must be compatible with both.

activities.title: Add, fill, switch, drop
activities.instruction: During a rolling deploy, old and new instances share one database. Renaming a column in one step breaks the old instances. Expand instead: add the new column (nullable), write to both, backfill, switch reads, then drop the old column in a later release.

activities.title: The one-step rename
activities.question: You rename `name` to `display_name` in a single migration during a rolling deploy. What happens?
choices: Instances still running the old code fail when they query `name`
The deploy waits for all instances to restart
Postgres keeps both columns automatically
activities.answer: Instances still running the old code fail when they query `name`
activities.explanation: The database is shared, so a migration applies to code that has not been updated yet. Expand/contract keeps every intermediate state readable by both versions.

activities.title: Write the expand step
activities.instruction: Write a migration that adds a nullable `display_name` column and an index on it.

teaching.text: A deploy is a race between versions. Migrations should be backward compatible for at least one release, and destructive changes belong to a later deploy than the code that stopped using them.

ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN display_name text;
CREATE INDEX users_display_name_idx ON users (display_name);
Run migrations as a separate step from app start when you can. Multiple replicas all trying to migrate at boot is a race you do not want to debug.

lessons.task: Write the additive migration for a rename.
lessons.starterCode: -- Expand: add the new column first
hints: Add the column as nullable and index it.

ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN display_name text;
CREATE INDEX users_display_name_idx ON users (display_name);
lessons.solution:
ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN display_name text;
CREATE INDEX users_display_name_idx ON users (display_name);
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why does a destructive migration belong in a later release than the code change?

lessons.title: 6. Zero-downtime deploys
lessons.summary: Start new instances only when ready, and let old ones finish their work.

activities.title: Ready is not alive
activities.instruction: A liveness probe says the process is up. A readiness probe says it can serve traffic — database reachable, migrations applied, caches warm. On shutdown, stop accepting new connections on SIGTERM, finish in-flight requests, then exit. The load balancer does the rest.

activities.title: What readiness checks
activities.question: What should `/readyz` report?
choices: Whether this instance can serve requests right now
Whether the process has started
Whether the last deploy succeeded
activities.answer: Whether this instance can serve requests right now
activities.explanation: Traffic routing keys off readiness. If it reports 'process started' while the database is unreachable, the load balancer sends users to a broken instance.

activities.title: Drain on shutdown
activities.instruction: Handle `SIGTERM` by closing the HTTP server and exiting once in-flight requests finish.

teaching.text: Zero downtime is a combination of three things: readiness before traffic, more than one instance during the swap, and a graceful drain after shutdown starts.
Match the drain timeout to your longest request. A 30-second job with a 10-second grace period is a failed request every deploy.

hints: Add a `/readyz` route that checks the database, and a SIGTERM handler that closes the server.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why does adding an instance before removing one remove most deploy downtime?

lessons.title: 7. Feature flags
lessons.summary: Ship the code dark, then choose who turns it on.

activities.title: A switch you can flip
activities.instruction: Deploying code and releasing a feature are different events. A flag lets the code reach production while behaviour stays off, enables it for internal users or a percentage, and turns it off in seconds if something looks wrong — without a deploy.

activities.title: Why flag it
activities.question: What is the main operational benefit of a feature flag?
choices: You can change behaviour without another deploy
It removes the need for tests
It makes the code smaller
activities.answer: You can change behaviour without another deploy
activities.explanation: Rollback becomes a config change rather than a build. That buys you a fast kill switch and gradual rollout at the same time.

activities.title: Put the new path behind a flag
activities.instruction: Wrap the new checkout in a flag check, falling back to the old one.

teaching.text: Flags separate risk into two decisions: is the artifact good, and is the feature ready. Treat the second one as data, with an owner and an expiry.
Delete flags once a rollout completes. A codebase full of stale switches is its own kind of outage.

lessons.task: Gate the new checkout path behind a flag.
hints: Check the flag first and keep the old implementation as the fallback.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why does a flag need an owner and an expiry date?

lessons.title: 8. Canaries and rollback
lessons.summary: Send a little traffic first, and decide with numbers.

activities.title: Five percent, then watch
activities.instruction: A canary sends a small slice of traffic to the new version and compares error rate and latency against the baseline. If the canary is worse, abort and keep the old version; if it matches, promote. This is only safe when the schema change works for both versions.
activities.example:
deploy:
  strategy: canary
  steps:
    - setWeight: 5
    - pause: 5m
    - analysis:
        metrics: [error_rate, p95_latency]
        abortOn: error_rate > baseline * 1.5
    - setWeight: 50
    - pause: 10m
    - setWeight: 100

activities.title: Rollback limits
activities.question: When is rolling back to the previous version unsafe?
choices: After a migration that dropped a column the old code still reads
When the previous image is more than a week old
Whenever the canary shows higher latency
activities.answer: After a migration that dropped a column the old code still reads
activities.explanation: Code rolls back; destructive schema changes do not. That is why the destructive step is separated into a later release.

activities.title: Write the canary stages
activities.instruction: Write canary steps that send 5%, pause, then 50%, then 100%, aborting on an error-rate spike.

teaching.text: Progressive delivery turns a binary deploy into a measurement. The automation should be able to stop itself; a human watching a dashboard at midnight will not.

metrics: [error_rate, p95_latency]
abortOn: error_rate > baseline * 1.5
Decide the abort threshold before you start. Choosing it while the graph is red is how teams talk themselves into an outage.

lessons.task: Write canary steps with an automatic abort rule.
hints: Set weights in stages, pausing between them.
lessons.solution:
deploy:
  strategy: canary
  steps:
    - setWeight: 5
    - pause: 5m
    - analysis:
        metrics: [error_rate, p95_latency]
        abortOn: error_rate > baseline * 1.5
    - setWeight: 50
    - pause: 10m
    - setWeight: 100
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why can automation abort a bad canary faster than a person can react?

lessons.title: 9. The release checklist
lessons.summary: Every release should be identifiable, documented and reversible.

activities.title: A tag, a note, a way back
activities.instruction: A release has a semantic version, a changelog entry written for humans, and a deploy record linking the version to the commit and the artifact digest. The checklist is short on purpose: it is the list of things that have caused incidents before.
activities.example:
# 1.4.2 — 2026-10-23

## Fixed
- Checkout retries no longer double-charge (idempotency key).

## Rollback
- `deploy --image ghcr.io/acme/api@sha256:previous`
- No migrations in this release.

activities.title: Which version bump?
activities.question: You remove a field from an API response that clients read. Which semver bump fits?
choices: Major
Minor
Patch
activities.explanation: Removing something clients depend on is a breaking change, so it is major. Adding a new optional field is minor; a fix is patch.

activities.title: Write the release note
activities.instruction: Write a release section with the version, a human changelog entry and a rollback line.

teaching.text: Traceability is the difference between 'something broke' and 'version 1.4.2 broke it at 14:02, here is the commit and the image'. It costs one line per release.

# 1.4.2

## Fixed
- ...

## Rollback
- deploy previous digest
Write the changelog for the person on call, not for the marketing site. What changed, what to watch, how to undo.

lessons.task: Write a release note with version, change and rollback.
hints: Include the version heading, what changed, and how to undo it.

# 1.4.2

## Fixed
- ...

## Rollback
- deploy the previous digest
lessons.solution:
# 1.4.2 — 2026-10-23

## Fixed
- Checkout retries no longer double-charge (idempotency key).

## Rollback
- `deploy --image ghcr.io/acme/api@sha256:previous`
- No migrations in this release.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why is a rollback plan the most valuable part of a release note?
